items.title: Five takeaways from Trump's midterm campaign rallies
items.content_html:
Oct 24 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump is in the midst of a nationwide campaign blitz ahead of the November midterm elections, holding near-daily rallies to boost turnout for Republicans who are fighting to keep control of Congress.

In his 90-minute stump speeches, Trump defends his economic policies, boasts about crowd size, mocks protesters and has even admired a fellow Republican’s buttocks.

Here are five takeaways from Reuters coverage of the president’s appearances, staged mostly in Republican-friendly areas across the country:

TRUMP'S ECONOMIC PITCH COLLIDES WITH VOTER REALITY

At the start of the month, Trump said he had done a “bad job” explaining his economic record. He has tried to remedy that at his rallies, pointing to a record-low poverty rate, low unemployment, record highs in the stock market and cheaper prices for some food items.

But his sales pitch is colliding with voters' concerns about how much they are spending on gas, groceries and other everyday expenses.

Consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged. The nationwide average price of gas is $4.27 per gallon ($1.13 per litre), nearly 40% higher than a year ago, according to AAA. Trump has repeatedly promised that gas prices will fall once the Iran war ends.

The disconnect was evident outside Trump's rally in rural Kansas, where Chester Daniel, a 90-year-old military veteran and Trump supporter, said the economy has “a long way to go” to help working people.

“Prices? Too high! We will never go back to what they were when this all started, but they need to come way down," Daniel said. "I don’t know how these young people make a living for their family."

RALLY MAP SHOWS REPUBLICANS PLAYING DEFENSE

Trump's travel map signals just how difficult it will be for Republicans to retain control of Congress, with the president forced to play defense deep in conservative territory.

Trump has traveled twice to Texas for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, campaigned for Republican Senate incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas and made two stops in Ohio for Senator Jon Husted. Trump also rallied for Republicans in competitive races in Alaska, Iowa, Montana and South Carolina. He is set to visit Mississippi on Monday.

Those are places Republicans are accustomed to winning easily, not battlegrounds where Trump would spend time during the crucial final weeks before an election.

Paxton narrowly trails Democrat James Talarico in polls, while Marshall faces a serious challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. Husted trails former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown in polls in Ohio, and Republican Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson is in a close race against Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa.

Notably absent from Trump's travels so far with less than two weeks until Election Day: Michigan, Maine, Minnesota and New Hampshire – also home to tight Senate races. He is soon poised to hit some of those locations. He is scheduled travel to Michigan on Sunday and has said he also plans to go to Maine.

TRUMP'S BOASTS ABOUT BIG CROWDS MEET UNEVEN REALITY

Trump has made crowd sizes a recurring theme of his midterm rallies, portraying packed arenas and thousands of people he says are stranded outside as evidence of his persisting popularity.

But actual turnout on the campaign trail in recent weeks has been uneven. Some rallies have drawn capacity crowds but have shown little sign of the overflow Trump described. At others, large sections of seats remained empty even in modest-sized venues.

"I'm doing these every night, and no matter where I go, it's the same thing. It's massive crowds," Trump said at a rally in North Carolina on Tuesday. "We have big screens outside. Thousands and thousands of people. There's something going on that's very special."

The venue was filled to capacity, but there were no signs of crowds outside waiting to get in or watching on screens.

At an October 7 rally in San Antonio, Texas, Trump said lines stretched two miles outside the arena even as sizable sections inside remained empty.

Crowd sizes are not always an accurate measure of political support, but Trump has pointed to them as a sign of strength even as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either of his presidential terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday.

Trump is not on the ballot on November 3. For Republican candidates, the question is whether the enthusiasm he generates among his supporters can translate into votes for them.

FRANCE BECOMES A 'BETE NOIRE' FOR MIDTERMS

Trump has often used French President Emmanuel Macron as a foil in his campaign stump speeches, claiming he strong-armed Macron into raising prescription drug prices in France by threatening tariffs on a popular French export, champagne, and other goods.

But in the last week or so Trump has seized on another narrative about France, casting its violent unrest of recent weeks as a warning of what he says could happen in the US if Democrats win in the midterms. Trump has blamed the unrest on migrants and Muslims, following a familiar playbook that has featured in his politics for more than a decade.

“What the hell happened to France?” Trump told a crowd in a livestock competition arena in Clemson, South Carolina, on Wednesday.

Notably, the French protests have taken a larger role in Trump’s recent speeches than two other major foreign policy headaches he has been unable to resolve: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and his war against Iran.

“They’ll end one way or another,” Trump said of the two conflicts at his Clemson rally. He did not elaborate on how they might end, but complained that he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work to resolve conflicts around the world.

TRUMP PUTS THE BODY IN BODY POLITIC

Trump has long had a fixation on the human physique that stretches beyond the body politic.

This campaign season, Trump has given particular attention to Husted, a 59-year-old former college football player for the University of Dayton.

At rallies in Ohio, Kentucky and North Carolina, Trump marveled at Husted’s physique, at one point saying his backside is “like a pile of muscle.”

“Then I looked at his legs, and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big.’ Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. It was like a piece of steel. I said, ‘This guy’s a monster,’” Trump said.

Trump had similar praise on Friday for Robert F. Kennedy Jr., his secretary of health and human services, telling a campaign rally in Florida that the 72-year-old "has the body of a 30-year-old."

Such riffs are familiar terrain for Trump. At the close of his 2024 campaign, he used a Pennsylvania rally speech to tell a crude story about PGA legend Arnold Palmer's prowess beyond his golf game. Trump's focus over the years on people's physical attributes has also included mocking the weight and looks of his opponents.

Trump finds even some of his friends lacking in fashion sense, including the rumpled Paxton.

"Some may not like the way he dresses," Trump said about him at the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas in mid-September, adding: "I don't."

That has not stopped Trump from campaigning for Paxton, however. He returns to Texas on Tuesday for two more campaign rallies.

items.title: Kamala Harris returns to US campaign trail with midterms, 2028 in view
items.content_html:
Oct 24 (Reuters) - Kamala Harris is returning to the campaign trail to help Democrats in some of the tightest US midterm races, putting the former vice president back before voters as she weighs whether to make a third run for the presidency in 2028.

The Democratic Party's unsuccessful 2024 standard-bearer has made relatively few public appearances this year. But with her party trying to break the Republican hold on Congress on November 3, Harris is rallying in Georgia, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and Wisconsin, a return likely to renew questions about her political future as a crowded field of potential 2028 contenders takes shape.

Harris kicked off her tour in Las Vegas on Tuesday with a new stump speech attacking what she described as the cruelty of President Donald Trump, mixed with the aspirational aphorisms that have long been her calling card as the first Black and Asian person and first woman to become vice president.

She spoke to scores of Culinary Workers Union members alongside gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford, Nevada's first Black attorney general, who she said would be the "first Black governor west of the Mississippi."

"We got a serious fight in front of us," Harris said. "We are witnessing pure brutality come out of what is undoubtedly the most corrupt, callous and incompetent presidential administration."

Like Trump, who is jetting around the country for Republican candidates, Harris is not broadly popular among voters. A Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll, opens new tab in June showed 39% of Americans viewed her favorably, but the figures were starkly partisan: 82% of Democrats viewed her favorably, compared to 7% of Republicans and 33% of independents.

"At the end of a campaign, you bring out your heavy hitters," said Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and a member of the Democratic National Committee. "That's what's going on here with her, and frankly with Trump."

The day after Las Vegas, Harris led chants of "Mississippi matters!" to a crowd supporting Scott Colom in the city of Columbus. Colom is seeking to become the first Democratic US senator elected in Mississippi since 1982, and polls show an unusually tight race with Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Harris opened with advice she said she gives young people she mentors: "Never let someone else's limited ability to see your capacity be a limitation on your ambition," she said. "Let me repeat that." And she did, louder than the first time, drawing cheers from the crowd.

UNDECIDED ON 2028

If Harris decides to run again for the White House in 2028, she would likely be among the most high-profile names in what is expected to be a crowded Democratic field.

But Harris also carries the baggage of past defeats: she lost the 2024 presidential election to Trump, and her first White House campaign ended before the 2020 Democratic nominating contests began.

A 2028 campaign would also force Harris to revisit the Democrats' chaotic 2024 race, when then-President Joe Biden abruptly ended his reelection campaign over questions about his health and mental acuity and she replaced him as the nominee.

Harris has since called Biden's decision to seek reelection "reckless" in her memoir "107 Days," a reference to the short campaign she inherited. This month, she offered her clearest criticism yet of his support for Israel's war in Gaza, rebuking the Israeli government's "horrific conduct" and saying the US should have "acted sooner and more forcefully."

"All these things will be relitigated," Kamarck said. "What happened to Biden? Did she know? Did she think he was losing it? And on and on and on."

Scott Ferson, a Democratic strategist and author of "How the Democrats Lost America," said the party has tended to give short shrift to candidates who have lost, though voters disillusioned with Trump may also view Harris in a new light.

"She has that kind of crossover appeal," Ferson said, "particularly with people who left in 2024 or stayed home." Her implicit message, he suggested, is "Do you regret staying home?"

This month, as she wrapped up an appearance, opens new tab on the "Baby, This Is Keke Palmer" video podcast, Palmer asked her if she would run again.

"Oh, girl, come on!" Harris said, laughing while gripping the hands of the Hollywood movie star. "I haven't decided yet."

"But the midterms, the midterms, the midterms," Harris went on. "2028 don't matter if we don't do 2026 right."

items.title: Trump foreign policy hits voters in the pocketbook, imperiling Republicans in midterms
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Foreign policy is rarely the deciding factor in US midterm elections, when economic considerations usually drive voters’ choices.

But this time, with Donald Trump’s war against Iran and his sweeping tariff campaign pushing up costs for Americans, a president’s approach to world affairs has itself become a pocketbook issue.

As the November 3 elections approach, there are growing signs that voters are drawing that connection directly, creating a major liability for Trump and his fellow Republicans and imperiling their control of Congress.

Those include a Reuters/Ipsos poll earlier this month showing some 78% of Americans blame Trump's policies for rising prices that are outpacing their earnings.

Not since 2006, when President George W. Bush’s Republicans lost both legislative chambers while he was mired in the unpopular Iraq war, has a US leader’s handling of international events appeared so central to shaping the midterms outcome.

The political backlash for Trump could be even bigger, with opinion polls showing that voters feel the economic pain from high gas prices and rising grocery bills in a way that they didn’t two decades ago.

“The bottom line is people are experiencing the impact of Trump’s war and other policies,” said Christopher Preble, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington. “Now voters have a chance to register their discontent with how he’s dealing with all this.”

POLITICS DRIVING FOREIGN POLICY

With Trump’s approval ratings touching historic lows, he has left little doubt, despite his public claims to the contrary, that he sees the straight line voters are drawing between his foreign policy and their cost of living.

That has prompted some controversial policy moves in the run-up to the elections.

Chief among them was Trump’s lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports aimed at bringing down fuel prices, a step his critics, including some fellow Republicans, say reinforces the impression that he is increasingly siding with Moscow in its war in Ukraine.

He has also pressed Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian refineries as he tries to shift the blame for high US gasoline prices despite experts saying the surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the war he launched alongside Israel against Iran nearly eight months ago.

At the same time, he has promised not to order any new attack on Iran before the midterms, though the US and Israel are widely reported to be preparing for a possible major escalation after the elections.

Polls have shown that most voters oppose the war initiated by Trump, who had campaigned on avoiding new foreign interventions. He has insisted Americans should accept temporarily higher gas prices so that he can block Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.

Iran says its nuclear program is for civilian purposes. The UN nuclear watchdog and US intelligence community have assessed that Tehran shuttered a nuclear weapons development program in 2003.

Some Republican candidates have distanced themselves from Trump on matters ranging from the conflict in the Middle East to the trade war with Canada and his pressure campaign against Ukraine.

For its part, Iran has sought to keep oil prices high and hurt Trump in the midterms by deploying new tactics to target ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and deliberately prolonging the diplomatic stalemate, senior Iranian officials have told Reuters.

Defending the administration's approach, White House spokesman Matt Middleton said: "President Trump has always been clear about temporary market disruptions as a result of the conflict in Iran, but the contrast between President Trump’s economic record and Democrats’ ruinous alternative is clear."

‘IT’S THE ECONOMY, STUPID’

Midterm elections historically have been seen as a referendum on the performance of the incumbent in the White House.

And in one election after another in recent decades, the conventional wisdom has been that economic concerns - “it’s the economy, stupid,” as the Clinton-era adage goes - dominate voters’ choices.

Opinion polls for this year’s midterms, including the Reuters/Ipsos survey, show that while voters rank foreign policy low on their list of priorities, it is clear that most Americans see some of Trump’s signature moves on the world stage, such as the Iran war and tariffs, feeding into their higher costs.

Other polls have shown that a majority of Americans have also soured more broadly on Trump’s international approach.

The Chicago Council on Global Affairs said its latest nationwide survey, opens new tab “finds that most Americans believe the Trump administration’s foreign policy actions have negatively impacted America’s global standing and hurt national and household economic conditions.”

Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has shaken up the rules-based global order that Washington helped create from the ashes of World War Two while his relations with allies have steadily worsened and the limits of US power have been increasingly exposed, analysts say.

LEGISLATIVE BALANCE OF POWER IN PLAY

Against this backdrop, Democrats are widely projected to gain control of the House of Representatives in the midterms, with the Senate also seen as increasingly in play.

For Republicans, losing either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his second term.

But even with a shift in the balance of power on Capitol Hill on November 3, lawmakers will have a hard time reining in Trump’s capacity to pursue foreign policy as he sees fit.

Once the ballots are counted, a big question will be whether Trump will feel either restricted or emboldened on the world stage as he enters what is traditionally considered a lame-duck phase - when a president is barred from running again and no longer faces electoral consequences for decisions made.

“For many presidents who feel politically constrained (at home), foreign policy is the area where they are able to act with relative freedom,” said Jon Alterman of the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank in Washington.

Analysts say Trump's handling of adversaries such as Iran, Russia, China and even Cuba or his approach to allies across the globe could go either way -- or he could simply lose interest and double down on his string of construction projects, such as the White House ballroom.

items.title: Divided over Israel, Detroit Democrats unite on rising costs for midterm elections
items.content_html:
DETROIT, Oct 24 (Reuters) - It was her son’s eighth birthday, but Dayna Broadnax could not afford a present.

Broadnax, a 42-year-old single mother of four in Detroit, said soaring gas and grocery prices left little money to pay the bills, let alone buy gifts or throw a birthday party.

“It’s hard to tell your kids that you don't have the funds right now to buy them a $3 bag of Skittles,” she said while watching her sons practice with a free basketball team at St. Suzanne Community Resource Center.

Ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, Broadnax’s concerns are widely shared in Detroit. Jewish, Muslim and Black voters interviewed by Reuters often put affordability ahead of disputes over Israel and Gaza, even as many expressed reservations about Democratic US Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

El-Sayed, who could make history as the first Muslim US senator, faces former congressman Mike Rogers in a competitive race that could help determine control of the Senate. A RealClearPolitics average gives El-Sayed a two-point lead – 48% to 46%.

Broadnax has yet to decide who to support, saying she will vote for the candidate most focused on lowering costs.

She sometimes skips meals so her children can eat and chooses which bills to pay after gas eats up at least $50 of the $150 she makes on a typical day driving for Lyft.

“Being a single mom, trying to take care of four boys out here in America now is too hard,” she said. “Whatever candidate whose main focus is affordability – that’s who I’m going with.”

But El-Sayed faces resistance from some voters who would ordinarily be inclined to support a Democrat, particularly over Israel.

“Both of the candidates have decided that this election is about Abdul,” said Matt Grossmann, a political science professor at Michigan State University. “He needs to win over voters that would normally support the Democratic candidate and are upset with President Trump but might have reservations about him – personal or policy reservations.”

El-Sayed’s challenge is not only keeping uneasy Democrats from voting for Rogers, but getting them to vote at all. Some voters told Reuters that opposing Trump made backing Rogers difficult, while concerns about El-Sayed led others to consider sitting out the race.

JEWISH VOTERS’ RESERVATIONS

Most Jewish voters in Detroit traditionally vote Democratic, but some have deep reservations about El-Sayed over his views on Israel, particularly his response to a March attack on a suburban synagogue. After a man rammed his truck into Temple Israel while more than 100 children were inside, El-Sayed drew backlash when he said “hurt people hurt people" in reference to the attacker.

Though El-Sayed later apologized for the comment, he has continued to draw heavy criticism from a community shaken by the attack.

Rabbi Aaron Starr of Congregation Shaarey Zedek said some Jewish men now cover their heads with baseball caps instead of yarmulkes because they fear being targeted if identified as Jews. Starr's synagogue spends twice as much on security measures for its sprawling campus following the attack.

Starr and a group of Jewish clergy launched a petition calling for the Democratic Party to agree to a set of “non-negotiable” principles, including acknowledging Israel’s right to exist and Jewish sovereignty in Israel. El-Sayed has not signed the petition or communicated with the group, Starr said. He said he would not vote for the Democratic nominee.

“He is hyper-focused on Israel and American supporters of the state of Israel and seemed to be placing an awful lot of blame on Israel for America's problems,” Starr said in his study, where “hurt people help people” yard signs leaned against a wall beside shelves of religious texts.

El-Sayed briefly campaigned with Hasan Piker, a left-wing streamer who has drawn criticism over comments about Israel and American Jews. The association has troubled some voters, while others remain more focused on the cost of living.

“I don't love the fact that he campaigned with Hasan Piker during the primary,” said Alicia Chandler, a 47-year-old Jewish Detroit resident and former supporter of El-Sayed's Democratic primary opponent Haley Stevens. “But it cost me almost $100 to fill my car with gas yesterday.”

El-Sayed has repeatedly pledged to protect Jewish people from antisemitism, saying in an August speech after winning the Democratic primary that his commitment to Jewish safety was “the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters.”

GAZA AND THE POCKETBOOK

In 2024, frustration with the Biden-Harris administration’s support for Israel’s war in Gaza drove many Arab American and Muslim voters in Michigan away from the Democratic ticket, with some backing the Republican Trump or third-party candidates and others choosing not to vote.

At Shibam Coffee, a Yemeni coffeehouse in the Arab-majority city of Dearborn, volunteers wearing “Abdul for Senate” shirts gathered over cardamom coffee, honeycomb bread and sambusas before heading out to canvass. The cafe is popular with young Arab Americans, many of whom now support El-Sayed.

Sumayah Dhalai, a 22-year-old senior at Wayne State University who plans to vote for El-Sayed, liked his policy position opposing funding for the Israeli government but said her fears about finding a job and affording rent and groceries were a bigger factor in deciding who to vote for.

“The overwhelming majority of us are very scared about graduating because everybody’s telling us that everything sucks,” Dhalai said. “As much as I want to say I'm out here fighting for world peace, I have to ensure my own ability to succeed before I can then turn to focus on everybody else's.”

While parts of Detroit have benefited from new investment, others have not, including the neighborhood housing St. Suzanne Community Resource Center, where the median household income is just $36,525 and roughly half the children live in poverty, according to US Census data.

“The financial stress is continual,” said Steve Wasko, the director of the center where Broadnax's sons play basketball. “Being able to pay your rent, afford your light bill, pay your mortgage, or pay to have your furnace working sufficiently – these are the most common requests that come through the door."

items.title: US accuses government contractor of leaking classified info to girlfriend's Substack
items.content_html:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department accused a government contractor on Friday of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, the publisher of a Substack newsletter.

The FBI arrested Ian Brinksman, 42, on Friday following a search of his Washington home, a Justice Department statement said. Prosecutors charged him with unlawfully transmitting national defense information.

A federal public defender representing Brinksman declined to comment.

“As alleged, Brinksman reached far outside his own duties to obtain some of our Nation’s most closely held secrets and handed them to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish them,” John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, said in the statement.

“That is not carelessness. It is a betrayal of his oath and the American people who entrusted him to fulfill his duties honorably,” Eisenberg said.

Brinksman held a top secret security clearance while working as an employee of a US government agency and later as a developer for systems integration for a private contractor working for the same agency, prosecutors said.

According to the sworn affidavit of an FBI agent investigating the case, Brinksman repeatedly accessed classified intelligence reports and then communicated with the journalist. The affidavit also cites phone records, database access logs, badge-swipe records, emails and other evidence.

The affidavit only identifies the journalist as "Individual 1," but it cites excerpts from articles she published.

"A fundraising article reportedly published by Individual 1 in September 2026 stated 'over the past year (Individual 1 has) published reporting based on classified (relevant U.S. government agency) assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about,'" the affidavit reads.

That quote appears in a September 28 piece, opens new tab published on the Capital & Empire online newsletter authored by Aída Chávez.

"Over the past year, I’ve published reporting based on classified CIA assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about," wrote Chávez, whose profile on the site notes that she worked for the Nation and other outlets before she launched the newsletter.

Chávez did not respond to an email message seeking comment.

Investigators allege that on at least five occasions in 2026, Individual 1 published Substack articles containing information that mirrored the classified reports, some at the top secret level. On some of those dates, Chávez published articles that cite classified reports, some of them attributed to the CIA.

According to a LinkedIn profile bearing Brinksman's name, he worked for Deloitte as a manager and as a senior strategy security consultant after having worked as a US State Department foreign service officer on dates corresponding to those outlined in the Justice Department statement.

The State Department declined to comment. Deloitte did not respond to requests for comment.

items.title: US congressional candidate Brad Lander released after being detained by Israeli military in West Bank
items.content_html:
TEL AVIV, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Brad Lander, a US Democratic Party candidate for Congress, was detained by Israeli forces in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday, along with other Americans and Israelis harvesting olives alongside Palestinian farmers, rights groups said.

Lander wrote on X that he had been released with a warning, which he said was apparently due to his public profile, but said several dozen rabbis and other participants were still detained.

"The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn't a crime under any law I know," he earlier posted, saying he had been detained by the military.

Lander, who is Jewish, was among a group of international volunteers, which one organiser said also included British and Canadian citizens, accompanying local Palestinian farmers as an act of solidarity in what is known as protective presence. The farmers often face the threat of violence from Israeli settlers.

Lander is a former New York City comptroller and mayoral candidate who is running for New York's 10th Congressional District in the US House of Representatives in the November 3 midterm elections. He is an ally of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and is critical of Israel's conduct in the war in Gaza.

The annual olive harvest is a cultural tradition and important source of income for Palestinians. It is also often the target of violent attacks carried out by Israeli militant settlers.

Israeli settler attacks against Palestinians and other civilians in the West Bank over the weekend prompted a call by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Saturday for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government to crack down on the violence.

"The story here is how hard the Israeli government works to make it impossible for Palestinian farmers to harvest their olive groves and drive on their roads and live in their homes and stay on their land," Lander said in a call with reporters from Beit Jala in the West Bank. "And I've had a chance to see that with my own eyes."

Lander said he was detained for about three hours, including the time spent being held at the harvest, while the others he was with were detained for about nine hours.

Israel's foreign ministry accused Lander of "looking for a confrontation" and said that he had ignored advice ahead of his visit that coordination with Israeli authorities was required.

In response, Lander said the Israeli embassy in DC had recommended coordination with local authorities but did not explicitly say it was necessary. He also said he had taken part in olive harvesting the previous two days without incident.

The incident took place in Nahalin, a village south of Bethlehem, as Palestinians were gathering olives accompanied by around 80 volunteers, according to Israeli organisation Rabbis for Human Rights and Jewish North American organisation T'ruah.

Israeli police said it had detained Palestinian olive harvesters and dozens of Israeli and foreign activists gathering olives near the fence of an Israeli settlement, saying it was prohibited. One of the foreign nationals was later released once it became known he was a congressional candidate, police said.

'HARVESTING OLIVES IS NOT ILLEGAL'

The military said harvesting in that area, which is located near the Israeli settlement of Beitar Illit, required prior coordination, which had not happened, and that those present had been detained. It did not say harvesting there was prohibited but that the "uncoordinated harvest" posed a security risk.

"We did not present a security risk to anyone. We did nothing more provocative than harvest olives," Lander said.

Mamdani wrote on X that Lander was among New Yorkers, including rabbis, who had been detained by Israel's government for accompanying Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest.

"Harvesting olives is not illegal. The occupation is," he said, accusing Israel of genocide, and demanding the release of the other New Yorkers and an end to the Israeli occupation.

Israel's government has denied accusations, including by a UN commission, and international and Israeli rights groups, that it is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

Police later said 72 people had been released, some on condition that they stay away from the harvest area. It also said four foreign nationals would face a hearing on Thursday to determine whether they would be deported.

Rabbis for Human Rights and T'ruah said Israeli military and police forces arrived around two hours after the Palestinians and volunteers began gathering olives, and informed them that they were in a closed military zone.

The participants were not aware it was a closed military zone and offered to leave, Rabbis for Human Rights Acting Director Anton Goodman had told Reuters by phone from the Beitar Illit police station, where he was being detained.

Israeli forces, however, said they were detaining the participants, who Goodman said accused them of disturbing the public before taking them to the police station.

T'ruah Chief Executive Rabbi Jill Jacobs, who was among those detained, said that before the Israeli forces arrived the volunteers had been picking olives with the Palestinian farmers "very peacefully".

"We were obviously not doing anything violent but just the very act of picking olives together with Palestinian farmers was apparently disturbing for some," said Jacobs, a 51-year-old rabbi from Manhattan, in a phone interview.

A spokesperson for the US Embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports that US citizens had been detained.

items.title: Insight: Inside the Trump-administration campaign to return Brazil’s Bolsonaro clan to power
items.content_html:
SAO PAULO, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Two US State Department officials led a campaign to restore the right-wing Bolsonaro clan to power in Brazil and successfully pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor, according to 10 current and former US officials with direct knowledge of the matter.

Their plan faces a reckoning on Sunday, when Senator Flavio Bolsonaro faces leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a tight run-off. Lula has warned Washington against encroaching on Brazil's sovereignty and accused his opponent of plotting with the Trump administration.

The two officials were Darren Beattie, a Senior Advisor for Western Hemisphere Affairs who oversees Brazil policy, and Ricardo Pita, another senior advisor promoted this year to Deputy Assistant Secretary for North America. The details of their campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power haven't been previously reported.

Beattie and Pita, both political appointees, operated with wide latitude to manage Washington's relationship with the second most-populous country in the Americas, the people said.

In the months before election campaigning began, they instructed US diplomats in Brazil that it was US policy to restore former President Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil’s leader – even though he had been disqualified from office for plotting a coup in 2022, when he lost the presidential election to Lula, three of the people said.

After Bolsonaro received a 27-year sentence in September 2025, the two men pivoted to supporting the candidacy of his son, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the three sources said. Beattie and Pita told embassy staff not to interact with other conservative presidential contenders who could challenge the younger Bolsonaro, they said.

Since last year, the two men have successfully advocated for punitive US government measures on Brazil designed to weaken Lula and boost the Bolsonaros, the 10 people told Reuters. The policies included designating Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups and imposing US sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court Justice who was spearheading the investigation into Jair Bolsonaro.

Reuters could not determine the extent to which the two men were acting on orders from the White House or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump, a vocal defender of Bolsonaro since his election defeat in 2022, hasn’t publicly endorsed any candidate.

The White House declined to comment and referred questions to the State Department.

State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott didn't answer questions about specific measures and directives involving Beattie and Pita but said in a statement: "All actions taken by the United States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to choose their leaders through free and fair elections."

Lula’s office did not respond to comment requests.

Orna Blum, one of the officials who spoke to Reuters about Beattie and Pita’s efforts, led the State Department's Brazil and Southern Cone office until retiring last year over her opposition to the Trump administration.

Washington "has every right to pursue its economic and strategic interests," she said. "But when American foreign policy instruments are used to pressure another democracy over the legal fate of a political ally, the line between diplomacy and political intervention has been crossed."

SANCTIONS ON A SUPREME COURT JUSTICE

Beattie is a former White House speechwriter fired in 2018 after addressing an event frequented by white nationalists. He’s also the architect of "free speech diplomacy, opens new tab," a policy advocated by Trump allies that seeks to punish nations they accuse of censoring right-wing speech by US citizens, companies and global right-wing allies.

The United States has accused Brazil Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes of violating free speech rights by jailing Brazilians for political social-media posts and by censoring content of US social-media companies. Moraes has argued he was ridding social media of fake news that undermined public faith in Brazil's democratic institutions.

Moraes did not respond to a comment request.

Pita, a conservative Venezuelan-American, is among many in Rubio's orbit who view Lula as a threat to US interests in Latin America. Rubio has been a key leader in the administration’s aggressive policy in the region, which has included an invasion of Venezuela to oust its president, an oil blockade of Cuba, and military attacks on suspected drug boats from Latin America.

Beattie and Pita were drawn to the Bolsonaro family’s right-wing politics, their antipathy towards Lula, and the idea that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of abuses by Brazil's Supreme Court.

Like Trump in the 2020 US election, Bolsonaro refused to concede he lost Brazil’s 2022 presidential vote, triggering riots by supporters who stormed government buildings. The Supreme Court convicted him in September 2025 of plotting a coup to remain in power.

Before the conviction, in early 2025, the Bolsonaros were aggressively lobbying Washington for sanctions under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act against Moraes, who had led criminal investigations into Jair Bolsonaro. The act is a 2016 federal law allowing US sanctions against foreign individuals responsible for human-rights abuses or severe corruption.

Around April 2025, Jair Bolsonaro’s younger son, Eduardo, visited Beattie in his State Department office in Washington DC, according to two former US officials. Eduardo Bolsonaro had been making the public case for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes since at least 2024, and in March 2025 he said in a livestream that it was "practically certain" the Trump administration would do so.

Eduardo Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment.

Beattie made calls to the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to appeal for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes, said a former US official with direct knowledge of the matter.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department administers Magnitsky sanctions through OFAC, offered no opposition, the former official said.

The US announced Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes in July 2025, citing his alleged violations of free-speech rights by censoring anti-government social-media posts.

A Treasury official said Bessent and Rubio are "fully aligned on the administration’s foreign policy."

TERRORIST DESIGNATIONS

The Bolsonaro family was also pushing for Washington to designate Brazil's top gangs – the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) – as terrorist organizations. They believed such a designation would hurt Lula, who some opponents have criticized for failing to control crime.

Eduardo Bolsonaro had become friends with Pita through US conservative circles, and both supported the effort to designate the gangs as terrorist groups.

In May 2025, Pita joined a US delegation, opens new tab that visited Jair Bolsonaro at his residence in Brasilia as he awaited his trial, according to public announcements at the time. Also in the group: David Gamble, the State Department’s top sanctions official at the time.

Back in Washington, Pita asked State sanctions officials to explore how terrorist designations like those announced against Mexican cartels in February 2025 could be used in Brazil, one former official said.

Nearly a year later, in May 2026 – after Pita was promoted to a new job that pulled him out of Brazil affairs – presidential contender Flavio Bolsonaro met with Beattie and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington to discuss "the urgency of designating the PCC and the Comando Vermelho as foreign terrorist organizations," according to an X post by right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo that included photos of the attendees.

The State Department announced the designation, opens new tab the following day.

Reuters could not determine the extent of Pita or Beattie’s influence in securing the final decision.

BACKFIRES AND SETBACKS

In July 2025, Washington also announced a series of other measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices' visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the "persecution" of Jair Bolsonaro.

Reuters could not determine what, if any, role Beattie or Pita played in the additional measures. But if they were intended to undermine Lula, many of them backfired, according to political analysts in Brazil.

Measures targeting the court did nothing to stop it from proceeding with Bolsonaro's trial, while the tariffs boosted the Lula government's poll numbers, the analysts said.

Major US and Brazilian firms reliant on bilateral trade – including meatpacking giant JBS (JBSS.O), opens new tab - controlled by Brazilian billionaires Wesley and Joesley Batista – also pushed back on the tariffs, which Washington eventually watered down.

Beattie and Pita’s campaign also hit setbacks. Without an official explanation from the Treasury Department, the US removed Justice Moraes from the Magnitsky sanctions list in December, and in March Brazil barred Beattie from entering the country to visit Bolsonaro in prison.

Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at risk intelligence firm RANE, said Trump may have decided to withhold a public endorsement of Bolsonaro to avoid being seen as meddling in Brazil's election – a perception that could boost Lula’s popularity.

Still, after Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outperformed Lula in the first-round election earlier this month, Trump called it a big victory.

"Close, but a very, very big victory," he told reporters. "Amazing, actually."

items.title: US blocks two devices with Chinese-made surveillance chips
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 22 (Reuters) - The Federal Communications Commission said on Thursday it had blocked two devices from the US market that contain foreign surveillance chips produced by a subsidiary of China's Huawei, the first time it had exercised authority under new rules.

The US telecom agency said it barred a dashboard camera and a wireless video transmitter containing chips produced by Huawei subsidiary HiSilicon, which the agency said advertises its chip as "designed for the surveillance market" and including "detection algorithms for human faces."

  • FCC Chair Brendan Carr said video devices containing surveillance chips produced by companies on its national security list "pose an obvious and unacceptable risk to the nation and our people."
  • Huawei did not immediately respond to a request for comment and HiSilicon could not immediately be reached.
  • The FCC voted in July to bar sales of devices in the US that contain key hardware from Chinese companies deemed to be national security risks
  • The Trump administration has mounted a sweeping crackdown on Chinese technology gear

items.title: Police officers resign after fatal shooting of Black child in Mississippi
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - A police officer in Mississippi who fatally shot a 1-year-old Black child in a Walmart parking lot in June and the interim police chief in the city where the shooting took place have resigned, local officials said on Friday.

Hunter Foster, the officer who shot the child, resigned from the Senatobia Police Department, Mayor Greg Graves said on Friday, without specifying whether he was asked to resign or did so on his own. Angelica Maze, who was the interim chief for the department, also stepped down, according to a resignation letter reported by local media.

Foster had fired his gun at a moving vehicle in response to a shoplifting call in Senatobia in June, killing 1-year-old Kohen Wiley. The fatal shooting of the child had sparked calls from civil rights advocates for accountability.

The child's family has said the shooting was not justified, but Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch said this week that "the use of force was justified" and cleared the officer of criminal wrongdoing.

Although Foster was cleared, his lawyer, Martin Zummach, told NBC News that his client "resigned for the good of the city and the police department and to permit the process of healing."

Prominent civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who is representing the child's family, said they were calling for a Department of Justice investigation and that accountability cannot end at the resignation of the officer.

The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation said after the shooting in mid-June that law enforcement officers responded to a shoplifting call at Walmart and encountered two adults and a juvenile child fleeing from the store into a vehicle.

Officers attempted to stop the vehicle, but the driver drove in their direction, the bureau added, saying that an officer "then discharged their weapon and the vehicle fled the scene."

Footage released from the incident showed Foster running out of the Walmart with other officers after an employee said suspected shoplifters were attempting to flee. While officials have alleged the child's mother and her friend stole diapers, the two women have not been charged.

"No mother should have to bury her baby over an allegation of shoplifting diapers," Crump said on Friday.

Former Senatobia Police Chief Harold Vanderford was fired, opens new tab in September after media outlets reported he used racist slurs against Black people in text messages.

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: Trump's approval falls to record low of 31% as midterms near, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's approval rating fell to a record low as Americans worried about high gasoline prices and appeared ready to punish his Republican Party in the November 3 congressional elections, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on Monday.

Some 31% of Americans approve of Trump's performance in office, down a percentage point from two weeks earlier and the lowest level in either of his presidential terms, the four-day poll showed.

Asked which party they would vote for if the congressional elections were held today in what is known as a "generic ballot" question, some 47% of registered voters in the nationwide poll picked Democrats and 35% chose Republicans. The 12-point Democratic advantage was the widest over the current election cycle and could bolster Democratic hopes of seizing control of the US House of Representatives and the US Senate.

For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his term.

Generic ballot polls are national polls that provide an overall view of which party poll respondents want to see in charge in Congress. While these polls provide a view of national public sentiment, they do not capture all the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House, contests in which Republicans hold some structural advantages.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll two weeks earlier showed Democrats leading Republicans by 7 points, 44% to 37%.

Much of the drop in support for Republican congressional candidates was due to a larger share of women saying they would pick Democrats. Some 50% of female voters said they would vote Democratic, compared to 32% eyeing Republican candidates. Men also favored Democrats, but by a smaller margin.

Trump's popularity has suffered since he ordered military strikes on Iran in February alongside US ally Israel. The war triggered a surge in gasoline prices, hitting household finances. Some 68% of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy, including 37% of self-identified Republicans.

Voters in the poll picked Democrats over Republicans as the better stewards of the economy, by 40% to 33%.

The survey, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,679 US adults, including 1,279 registered voters. The poll's results had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all respondents and 3 points for registered voters.

items.title: Midterms: Your questions, answered
items.content_html:
Oct 23 - Over the summer, we asked you to submit your most pressing questions about the US midterm elections. You asked about voter eligibility checks, threats to election officials or results, the effects of redistricting and which races are most likely to determine control of Congress.

Here are Reuters reporters’ answers to these questions, which were also published in the Politics US Newsletter. Similar questions have been combined and edited for clarity.

If you have more questions related to the midterms or other topics related to US politics, write to campaigntrail@thomsonreuters.com, opens new tab.

Q: Which national issues are having the greatest influence on competitive races?

Answered by: Nathan Layne, Politics Reporter, and Jason Lange, Politics Data Reporter

Our Reuters/Ipsos polling suggests that rising prices, exacerbated by the war with Iran, are having an outsized impact on the midterm environment. About half of voters say the cost of living is the single most important issue in the congressional elections, compared with roughly 1 in 5 who cite democratic norms and about 1 in 10 who point to immigration.

That focus on inflation extends across the major expenses that dominate household budgets, from housing and healthcare to food and fuel. Gasoline prices, pushed higher by the conflict, and the elevated cost of grocery staples such as coffee and beef are particularly potent politically because voters encounter them regularly at the pump and checkout counter.

Starting this past summer, our polling has shown that, for the first time in a decade, voters view Democrats as better stewards of the economy than Republicans. Against that backdrop, Republican strategists and party officials say they are seeking to frame the midterms as a choice between two parties, casting Democrats as increasingly influenced by socialist ideas, rather than a referendum on current economic conditions.

Q: What are the most plausible paths for Democrats and Republicans to win control of the House and Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, and which races are most likely to determine the outcome?

Answered by Jason Lange, Politics Data Reporter

Democrats face an uphill fight to win the Senate, where they need to pick up four seats. They would have to hold Michigan and New Hampshire – both tight races – while flipping four of six Republican-held seats in play: Alaska, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa and Texas – the last two of which haven't elected Democrats to the Senate in over a decade.

Republicans face more pressure in the House, where their 218 members hold the smallest possible majority in the 435-seat chamber. About three dozen races nationwide are competitive. Democrats' best pickup chances include Republican-held seats in Nebraska's 2nd District, New Jersey's 7th and California's 48th, where district boundaries were redrawn to favor Democrats. Democrats must also defend Ohio's 9th and North Carolina's 1st, both redrawn to favor Republicans.

Q: What procedures do states use to verify voter eligibility and citizenship, and what does the available evidence show about the frequency and detection of ineligible voting or other election fraud?

Answered by Joseph Ax, National Affairs Correspondent

Under federal law, every state must retain a statewide list of registered voters and perform regular maintenance on it to remove ineligible voters. In addition, US law requires first-time voters in federal elections who registered by mail to show some form of identification at the polls, such as a driver’s license, a paycheck or a utility bill.

Many states have imposed additional, more stringent procedures to verify eligibility, such as photo ID requirements, and those policies vary significantly among states. Votes cast by mail, which have come under frequent baseless attacks from Trump as unreliable, are typically checked by comparing the signature on the envelope with the one on file.

All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including noncitizen voting, is exceedingly rare. A Reuters investigation this year found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud.

The conservative Heritage Foundation think tank maintains a voter fraud database that includes just 1,619 cases from 1982 to 2025, or one for every 817,625 votes cast in a presidential election during that time.

Q: How are election officials preparing for threats to poll workers, misinformation, administrative disruptions or attempts to interfere with voting and vote counting?

Answered by Peter Eisler, Ned Parker, Linda So andMike Spector

Reuters interviewed more than 50 state and local election officials from both political parties, including a dozen secretaries of state, the top election officials in their states. Nearly all said they are adopting new strategies to prepare for political interference, misinformation, cyberattacks and even threats of violence ahead of the midterms. Their efforts span jurisdictions large and small, in areas controlled by Republicans and Democrats. In Michigan, for example, state officials are advising local clerks on the appropriate response if the federal government demands access to voting machines.

Preparations fall into three categories. Some election officials are hiring lawyers or seeking legal skills, as over a dozen interviewees said. Twice that many election officials said they are expanding public outreach and social media campaigns to counter misinformation around the reliability of mail-in voting or voting machines. Most of the interviewed officials said they are scrambling to fill gaps left by the Trump administration’s cuts to programs that help safeguard elections from cyberattacks and physical security threats. That includes ongoing work to fortify election offices with camera systems and bulletproof glass – a trend that began after Trump disputed his loss to Biden in the 2020 election, prompting violent threats by Trump supporters against election workers.

Read our reporting on more specific examples of what election officials are doing in preparation for such potential scenarios in Wisconsin, North Carolina, Georgia, Michigan, Colorado and Maine.

Q: How has redistricting affected the 2026 electoral map, and which maps or election practices are currently facing legal challenges?

Answered by Joseph Ax, National Affairs Correspondent

Nine states have new US House maps in place after the redistricting war that unfolded over the last year. Republicans were the clear winners: the party gained an advantage in 15 districts across those states, while Democrats improved their chances in only 6 districts. However, Democrats remain favored to win the House, with Trump’s weak approval ratings dragging down his party’s candidates.

There are about 40 seats in play in November out of 435 nationwide, meaning that a small fraction of voters will likely determine which party controls the House.

While some of the maps still face legal challenges, none of the litigation appears likely to alter any district lines ahead of November’s election.

Reuters reporters Bianca Flowers,David Hood-Nuño and Ally J. Levine mapped how redistricting has affected communities in Memphis, Tennessee.

items.title: Trump signs order aimed at reducing single-family housing costs
items.content_html:
Oct 22 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump on Thursday signed an executive order aimed at reducing expenses for homeowners by lowering insurance premiums, refinancing costs and interest rates on certain government-backed home loans, the White House said.

High home prices and elevated mortgage rates have put pressure on the Trump administration to deliver meaningful relief as affordability has emerged as a political vulnerability for Republicans ahead of the November midterm elections.

Trump's order directs the Federal Housing Finance Agency to launch a pilot program to cancel borrowers' mortgage insurance premiums once they meet equity requirements based on current market values. It also makes permanent an FHFA pilot program waiving title insurance requirements for mortgage refinancings.

In addition, the order establishes a task force on manufactured housing innovation to expand factory-built homes eligible for federal housing programs, and directs the agriculture and veterans affairs secretaries to reduce interest rates on single-family home loans issued by their departments.

Contracts to buy previously owned US homes plunged to a record low in September as rising mortgage rates depressed demand for housing, according to the National Association of Realtors.

US single-family housing starts fell 4.6% in September, while permits for future construction dropped 4% to their lowest level in 3-1/2 years, underscoring the challenges facing the housing market as borrowing costs rise.

The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate last week reached 7.40%, the highest in about three years, before falling to 7.32% this week, according to Freddie Mac. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which acts as a pricing benchmark for mortgages, has fallen by more than a quarter percentage point in the last two weeks.

items.title: US Treasury drops Venezuela from countries facing outbound US investment restrictions
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 22 (Reuters) - The US Treasury Department on Thursday announced proposed rules for screening outbound investment in China, Russia and other countries, a list that no longer includes Venezuela now that the country's former president Nicolas Maduro is not in power.

Treasury will accept comments through December 7 on the proposed rules, which were mandated under the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025, or COINS Act, that passed Congress in December, but grew out of a bipartisan effort first begun under former President Joe Biden in 2023.

The COINS Act marked a significant expansion of US outbound investment controls, requiring US firms and individuals to notify Treasury about certain investment plans while banning them outright in other cases to prevent harm to US national security. It expanded the covered countries and added biotechnology as one of the restricted sectors, giving Treasury the authority to add additional sectors as needed.

The outbound program initially targeted China alone, but the COINS legislation expanded the list of countries "of concern" to include Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia and Venezuela "under the regime of Nicolas Maduro."

But Treasury said it dropped Venezuela since Maduro's government "no longer exists" following the capture of the former president by US forces in January, adding that the current government, led by Maduro's deputy, Delcy Rodriguez, did not meet the definition. The proposed rule could still apply to certain investments in Venezuelan entities, Treasury said, without elaborating.

President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping for a lavish state visit to Washington last month, and has pursued a less restrictive approach on Chinese technologies in his second term, but Thursday's release of the proposed rules may signal a desire to keep some pressure on Beijing's tech ambitions.

"The idea behind the outbound program is to ensure that we have the ability to monitor and potentially prohibit the types of investments" that pose risks to US national security, Treasury Assistant Secretary Chris Pilkerton, who oversees investment security issues, told Reuters.

"It's not just about the investment itself; it's not just about the money. It's about the network, the supply chain, and things like that that come from that investment," he said, adding that such a complex web of relationships would be hard to regulate otherwise through export controls or other measures.

Treasury said the proposed rules would not ban all investments in countries of concern. Instead, they would target specific investments in entities that engaged in dual-use technologies that benefited military programs, surveillance states and countries with human-rights abuses.

The proposed rules require notification about prospective investments in six sectors and five designated countries, while banning them outright in the case of artificial intelligence.

They allow certain exceptions, including investments in publicly traded companies and transactions valued at less than $50,000. The proposal would also allow investors to request exemptions for transactions deemed to be in the national interest of the United States, Treasury said.

Treasury also added an additional sector -- biotechnology -- to the five identified in the legislation: advanced semiconductors and microelectronics; artificial intelligence systems; quantum information technologies; high-performance computing and supercomputing; and hypersonic systems.

It said certain advanced biotechnologies could pose an acute risk to national security, citing the proliferation of biological weapons, the development of brain-computer interfaces and harm to US supply chain security.

The rules do not include potential licensing agreements made by US pharmaceutical companies with China, a Treasury official said, meeting a key demand of major drugmakers like Pfizer (PFE.N), opens new tab.

The proposed rules ban investments in artificial intelligence technologies in the target countries. Treasury said it decided on the ban given rapid advances over the past two years that raised questions about the efficacy of "regulating or even distinguishing the most advanced models."

items.title: US to introduce label for all American-made seafood
items.content_html:
FORT MYERS, Florida, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said on Friday the United States would introduce a label for all American-made seafood to help inform people's choice about where the goods come from.

  • Kennedy made the announcement at a political rally with President Donald Trump in Fort Myers, Florida
  • The "U.S. Caught Seafood" label proposed by the Food and Drug Administration would be voluntary, the White House said in a statement
  • The Trump administration also launched a new website Seafood.gov for US fishermen and consumers about federal seafood initiatives, the White House said

items.title: US farm secretary says USDA reorganization blocked by judge is 'full bore ahead'
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 22 (Reuters) - US Secretary of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said on Thursday that the Department of Agriculture is "full bore ahead" on an agency reorganization that was blocked by a federal judge last week.

The USDA has planned to relocate thousands of employees outside of the Washington region and consolidate other regional offices as part of the President Donald Trump administration's overhaul of the federal branch.

A federal judge October 13 blocked the effort at several USDA agencies, ruling that the agency was "reprogramming" congressional funds for the reorganization, or using money for a different purpose than it was intended.

"We are full bore ahead in the reorganization," Rollins said on a call with reporters. "We believe in it more today than we ever have."

The USDA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

items.title: US Supreme Court to review 1868 federal ban on home distilling of liquor
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - The Supreme Court agreed on Monday to decide the legality of a federal ban on the home distilling of alcoholic spirits that was enacted in 1868 after the US Civil War to crack down on liquor tax evasion.

The dispute pits Republican President Donald Trump's administration, which is defending the law, against challengers who argue that the home-distilling prohibition exceeds the authority of Congress under the US Constitution. More than a dozen Republican-led states have backed the legal challenge to the statute.

The Supreme Court took up the administration's appeal of a lower court's decision against the ban. The justices are expected to hear arguments in the case and issue a ruling by the end of June.

Following the Civil War of 1861-1865, Congress sought to protect federal revenue by passing a law that banned home distilling. The current version of the law subjects violators to up to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine.

Challenges to the ban's legality have led to a split among lower federal courts of appeals.

In April, the New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals declared the law unconstitutional, calling it an unnecessary and improper means for Congress to exercise its power to tax. Days later, the Cincinnati-based 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the constitutionality of the law, saying it was a "necessary and proper means" of collecting federal excise tax on distilled spirits.

The dueling decisions prompted appeals to the Supreme Court by the Justice Department and legal challengers.

Attorneys general from 15 Republican-led states, including Ohio, Florida and Idaho, filed a Supreme Court brief backing the challengers to the federal ban and urged the justices to resolve the division, or "split," between the circuit courts of appeals.

"Unlike a good whiskey," the attorneys general wrote, "this split will not age well."

The 5th Circuit ruling was a legal victory for the nonprofit Hobby Distillers Association and 4 of its 1,300 members who argued in court papers that people should be free to distill spirits at home, whether as a hobby or for personal consumption.

Robert Alt, president and chief executive officer of the Buckeye Institute think tank and a lawyer for the challengers, expressed enthusiasm that his clients "will have their day in court."

"Our country's founders would be rolling over in their graves to learn that a pastime in which even George Washington partook, which is as American as apple pie and certainly a lot older, has quite absurdly been turned into a federal crime," Alt said.

The 5th Circuit upheld a 2024 ruling by US District Judge Mark Pittman in Fort Worth, Texas. The ruling barred federal authorities from enforcing the ban against the plaintiffs in that case.

The Justice Department, urging the justices to take up the case, emphasized the importance of protecting federal revenue.

"Congress restricted home distilling 160 years ago in response to an extensive history of evasion of the distilled-spirits tax," Justice Department lawyers wrote.

"The government has a substantial interest in its authority to safeguard a significant source of tax revenue — a source that was used to pay Revolutionary War debts at the founding (of the nation) and now generates billions of dollars in tax revenue every year," they wrote.

items.title: Rubio says Trump to take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions
items.content_html:
Oct 17 (Reuters) - The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation.

Rubio said on Saturday that the president will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlier.

"A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida.

In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump wrote that his decision-making was aimed at avoiding anything "that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table."

Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham Act, which he signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine.

The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next week. Friday's order did not specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump opted for a 60-day review.

"I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan.

Friday's executive order drew criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who warned it would embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war.

DIESEL SUPPLIES

Rubio on Saturday also defended a separate US agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies.

"That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get."

Under the agreement, Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States, followed by shipments in November and beyond.

The diesel agreement is "a carrot to try to end the war, not an economic lifeline" to Russia, US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said during a Sunday interview on ABC's "This Week."

But "the only way they can get additional diesel to export is if they turn down the conflict with Ukraine," Wright told CNN's "State of the Union" program on Sunday.

“If Russia can bring additional diesel to the market and export it, it would benefit American consumers,” he told CNN. “He's putting pressure that would both benefit American consumers and be a step forward for peace in the Russia-Ukraine war.”

Rubio said the diesel deal and sanctions waiver reflected the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies.

"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," he said.

items.title: New York City bans horse-drawn carriages from June 2028
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Oct 22 (Reuters) - The New York City Council voted on Thursday to ban horse-drawn carriages from city streets and Central Park beginning in June 2028, ending a historic tourist attraction and long-standing industry.

Out of the city's 51 lawmakers, 40 supported the bill, which was backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who earlier this month said the horse-drawn carriage industry would come to an end. Seven council members voted against it and two abstained.

Support for the ban grew after the death this summer of Romanch Mahajan, an 18-year-old tourist from India. Mahajan was thrown from a carriage and died on June 17, when the horse bolted after the driver stepped away to take a picture of Mahajan's family.

President Donald Trump, who has both attacked Mamdani and held cordial meetings with him, expressed skepticism about the ban.

"When there is a car accident in the area, of which there are many, they don't stop cars from entering the Park. So why would they stop the Carriages? It was a Great Tradition. Another piece of History that’s gone. It will be missed!" Trump, whose business empire is headquartered in Trump Tower, minutes from Central Park, wrote on Truth Social.

The bill requires the city to develop a transition plan for the workforce by April and to consider a program to compensate carriage operators for their businesses and help with the disposition of their horses. Under the proposal, the horses could not be slaughtered.

The day before the vote, the Transport Workers Union, which represents carriage business owners and drivers, said that if the bill is enacted, it will seek a temporary restraining order from a court "the minute the ink dries," according to a letter sent to New York City Corporation Counsel Steve Banks.

"This may be the first time in City history that a previously licensed profession was banned," the letter signed by principal attorney Arthur Schwartz said. "The proposed bill deprives the owner of all economically beneficial or productive use of their property."

items.title: NEWSLETTER: Trump's midterm calculus scrambles Ukraine policy
items.content_html:
Oct 22 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump has not so quietly shifted course on a major policy issue in the past month. After criticizing Russian President Vladimir Putin, he's started to make nice. What explains the turnabout? The November midterms may offer a clue.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, once Washington's most celebrated wartime ally, is finding himself caught in the crossfire of US midterm politics. He is under mounting pressure from Trump to strike a peace deal with Putin.

With US voters increasingly frustrated by high energy prices and the cost of living, Trump has turned renewed attention to the war in Ukraine in recent days, arguing that a negotiated settlement there could help ease economic pressures at home, even though US consumers would be unlikely to feel the effects of any peace deal ahead of the November 3 vote.

Trump has said the war may be closer than ever to finishing and that he wants the death and destruction to end. But he also may be betting that a resolution of the four-year conflict could ease pressures on the US economy, voters’ pocketbooks and his own political fortunes. Russia is a major oil supplier and has held out the possibility of a broad economic pact with Washington.

In recent weeks, Trump has cut a deal with Putin, temporarily easing US sanctions on Russian diesel (and waiving others) in exchange for Moscow providing more diesel to global markets. He’s considering a meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month, without Zelenskiy. Meanwhile, Kyiv has complained that a satellite system made by US-based SpaceX has stopped working when mounted on fast-moving drones, limiting its ability to strike Russian targets and defend against attacks.

The moves are a shift from Trump’s earlier criticisms of Putin and a return to more prickly relations between the US and Ukrainian leaders. Ukraine and several European allies have expressed alarm at an apparent pivot by Trump.

Trump has blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries for driving up global diesel prices. He’s also suggested that Ukraine needs a new leader. “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” he told us at the White House on Monday. “Zelenskiy is not helping matters much.” Trump envoy Steve Witkoff later called Putin a “humanitarian” for freeing a retired US schoolteacher in custody since 2022.

The Ukrainian attacks have contributed to higher diesel prices, although market analysts attribute most of the increase to disruptions in fuel shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. That’s a consequence of a different war: the US-led one with Iran.

Trump wouldn’t be the first politician to lay blame for inflation abroad. His Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, pointed to Putin after Russia's invasion of Ukraine caused gasoline prices to surge ahead of congressional elections in 2022.

Voters are not buying a similar argument from Trump. Some 78% of Americans say his policies bear at least some blame for rising prices, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll. Most Republicans and Democrats cited the cost of living as their top concern.

Zelenskiy told visiting US lawmakers on Monday that recent “decisions on the American side … are hard to explain.”

For the answer, he may need to look no further than the US political calendar.

TOP US POLITICS HEADLINES

  • Graphics: What redistricting means for Tennessee voters

  • US Supreme Court rulings reshape midterm election battlefield
