POLL OF THE WEEK

Your questions on election officials’ preparations for violent or legal threats

How are election officials preparing for threats to poll workers, misinformation, administrative disruptions or attempts to interfere with voting and vote counting?

Reuters interviewed more than 50 state and local election officials from both political parties, including a dozen secretaries of state, the top election officials in their states. Nearly all said they are adopting new strategies to prepare for political interference, misinformation, cyberattacks and even threats of violence ahead of the midterms. Their efforts span jurisdictions large and small, in areas controlled by Trump’s Republican Party as well as the opposition Democratic Party. In Michigan, for example, state officials are advising local clerks on the appropriate response if the federal government demands access to voting machines.

Preparations fall into three categories. Some election officials are hiring lawyers or seeking legal skills, as over a dozen interviewees said. Twice that many election officials said they are expanding public outreach and social media campaigns to counter misinformation around the reliability of mail-in voting or voting machines. Most of the interviewed officials said they are scrambling to fill gaps left by the Trump administration’s cuts to programs that help safeguard elections from cyberattacks and physical security threats. That includes ongoing work to fortify election offices with camera systems and bulletproof glass – a trend that began after Trump disputed his loss to Biden in the 2020 election, prompting violentthreats by Trump supporters against election workers.

Read our reporting on more specific examples of what election officials are doing in preparation for such potential scenarios in Wisconsin, North Carolina, Georgia, Michigan, Colorado, and Maine.

THE VIEW FROM PARIS

The French government is bracing for the prospect of more protests as soon as this weekend after some of the worst urban tumult in years. Thousands were arrested, and shops looted, amid nationwide protests on October 17 over high prices and declining public services. Trump has weighed in repeatedly on the crisis, blaming immigrants and radical Islam for the violence, without providing evidence. In Kansas on Monday, Trump warned voters that the US would burn like France if Democrats win. Macron shot back that Trump and other foreign leaders had spread misinformation about what happened and were looking to score political points at France's expense. He called comments by foreign leaders "stupid" and "unacceptable."

items.title: Meta has strong chance of getting $25 billion New Mexico penalty slashed on appeal, experts say
items.content_html:
Oct 22 (Reuters) - Meta Platforms (META.O), opens new tab has a strong basis for arguing that the $25 billion penalty New Mexico secured this week in a case stemming from allegations the firm mishandled user data should be reduced on appeal, legal experts said.

The judgment was one of the largest state verdicts against a company in US history. It came after a jury found Meta misled consumers about who had access to their data in the wake of revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a political consulting firm involved in President Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, had harvested personal data from millions of Facebook users.

New Mexico said state law allowed for a penalty of up to $5,000 for each time someone in the state may have seen an allegedly misleading statement from Meta. Experts said the company would likely argue that Judge Francis Mathew should only have considered people who actually saw the statements.

"The most vulnerable basis on appeal is going to be the question about whether a violation is going to count, even in the absence of any proof that a particular person saw one of these misrepresentations or relied on them to their detriment," said Peter Ormerod, a law professor at Villanova University.

C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal. The company is expected to appeal the underlying jury verdict and the penalty.

Meta has previously said that it does not sell user data and that New Mexico did not prove any consumer had actually been misled and that a penalty in the billions of dollars would risk violating its constitutional rights to due process and protection from excessive fines.

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday he expected Meta to appeal the judgment and the state stood ready to defend its legal position. He did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.

JURY FOUND 43 MILLION VIOLATIONS

New Mexico's attorney general sued Meta in 2021, alleging that the company lied to Facebook users about who had access to their data, how the company handled hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform, and other internal policies.

Jurors on September 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. Multiplying those statements by their potential audience within New Mexico, the jury said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection laws. The state had 1.4 million active Facebook users and a population of 2.1 million as of 2020.

Mathew said in his ruling on Wednesday that a penalty of more than $219 billion would be justified under state law, which allows a $5,000 penalty for each violation, but he reduced the amount.

The state had urged Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion, while Meta said penalties of no more than $3.45 billion were warranted.

Ormerod said that even if the company's appeals in state courts fail, Meta could argue to the US Supreme Court that the penalty violated its rights under the US Constitution to due process and against excessive fines.

The size of the penalty on its own does not mean it will be overturned, given the New Mexico law allowing for penalties for each willful violation, said Daryl Lim, a professor at Penn State Dickinson Law.

But it seems implausible that Meta was really responsible for so much financial harm, a sign the penalty may be unjust, said Eric Goldman, a professor at Santa Clara University School of Law.

"It felt like there was a lot of duplicative counting in the calculations," Goldman said. "How many times can a single person be duped by the same entity?"

items.title: Top RFK Jr. adviser Calley Means quits Trump administration
items.content_html:
Oct 22 (Reuters) - Calley Means, a close aide to US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., is resigning from his role as a senior adviser in the Trump administration, he said in a post on X on Thursday.

Means, who has been particularly active in the Kennedy-led “Make America Healthy Again,” submitted his resignation to Kennedy on Wednesday, a source familiar with the situation told Reuters.

"It was an honor to advocate for MAHA moms in the administration and steer policies like Dietary Guidelines reform, psychedelic reform, removing soda from SNAP, removing food dyes, GRAS reform, and overhauling government food procurement," Means said in his post on X.

He added that he is resigning from the White House with "tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy."

Means stepped into a permanent role as senior adviser supporting food and nutrition policy in November last year. Before that, he served as an adviser in the Trump White House from March to October as a special government employee.

The Wall Street Journal, which first reported his resignation earlier on Thursday, said Means was significantly frustrated by White House delays of some of Kennedy’s most popular policy ideas and blamed others in the administration for allowing food companies and special interests to have too much sway, citing people familiar with the matter.

The Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

His sister, Casey Means, also a key ally of Health Secretary Kennedy, had her nomination for US surgeon general withdrawn by President Donald Trump earlier this year.

items.title: In Iowa stronghold, Trump urges Republicans to turn out and vote
items.content_html:
SIOUX CITY, Iowa, Oct 22 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump on Thursday tried to galvanize Republican voters in Iowa, a state he won by double digits two years ago but now faces a tougher battle in the November midterm elections due to dissatisfaction with rising prices and the Iran war.

The Midwestern stop is part of Trump's push through states Republicans usually expect to win, but where polling points to some tight races.

Trump held a rally in Sioux City as Republicans defend a Senate seat, three House districts and the governor's office, giving Democrats an opening after years of Republican gains.

"Pretend I'm on the ballot, because if you get out, we're going to win big," Trump told the crowd gathered in an airport hangar.

He has spoken repeatedly with confidence about his connection with voters, though his approval rating has fallen and some Republicans Trump is trying to help have broken with him over the Iran war, as higher fuel and grocery prices deepen voters' economic worries.

Republican Representative Ashley Hinson, who also addressed the Sioux City rally, has called for an "immediate end" to the war, saying Iowans should not bear higher fuel or grocery prices because of it. She is in a close Senate race against Democratic state Representative Josh Turek.

"If we lose this seat here in Iowa, the Democrats will control the US Senate. Mark my words," she said on Thursday.

Republican Representatives Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, facing difficult reelection races, joined Democrats last month in voting to limit Trump's war powers in Iran.

"The only thing is the fuel prices that are hurting him more than anything," said rally attendee Ron Sitzmann, 73, a semi-retired parts and service director for an automotive company in Iowa, adding that he thought prices would drop once the conflict ended.

"I just wish it would happen sooner than later because it’s kind of dragging on," said Sitzmann, who remains a strong Trump supporter.

'PREACHING TO THE CHOIR'

Trump was in Iowa to back his party's candidates but used the platform to attack Democrats from other states, including Somali American Minnesota lawmaker Ilhan Omar, suggesting that she should quit Congress in the wake of a raid by federal agents on her home.

Omar says the government is being weaponized to target her as a political enemy of Trump's, who has been ramping up anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric in recent weeks.

In the Iowa races, Democrat Rob Sand leads Republican Zach Lahn in recent polling for governor, while Democrats are targeting an open House seat in the state's second congressional district.

Republican losses would be a setback for Trump in a state where his popularity helped the party build a commanding advantage.

The Senate and House races could help decide control of Congress, shaping his ability to advance his agenda during his final two years.

Republicans also worry about rural voters who powered Trump's Iowa victories, with farmers facing higher costs and trade uncertainty.

A Marist poll, opens new tab this month found 42% of likely voters said their finances had worsened over the past year, including more than half of independents. Thirty-five percent viewed their vote as a vote against Trump, versus 21% who saw it as a vote for him.

Trump's Iowa stop follows rallies earlier this week in Kansas for Senator Roger Marshall and South Carolina for Senator Darline Graham, where the Republicans are defending seats.

"We know he’s preaching to the choir," said Harlan Grau, 70, a staunch Trump supporter and pig farmer from Iowa. The rallies encourage supporters to "go out and get them 10 people to go to the polls with us," he added.

Trump's campaign swing comes as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either presidential term, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released Monday. The survey found 68% of Americans disapproved of his handling of the economy.

At recent rallies, his economic message has largely avoided the financial pressures facing many Americans. The Iran war has driven up gas prices, compounding broader cost-of-living concerns, while Trump has repeatedly promised prices will fall when the conflict ends.

Behind the scenes, Trump has questioned campaign spending, criticized redistricting efforts and second-guessed candidate choices, according to people familiar with the matter.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle rejected the people's characterizations, saying they were "armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation." Publicly, Trump has noted the tendency of a president's party to lose seats in midterm elections.

items.title: As Trump's support slips, white evangelicals remain his Republican bedrock
items.content_html:
BLYTHEWOOD, South Carolina, Oct 22 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump is losing ground among many of the voters who returned him to the White House in 2024. But Reuters/Ipsos polling and interviews with white evangelical Christians show they remain his most reliable constituency and could prove crucial in the November 3 midterm elections.

With Republicans on the defensive amid record-low approval ratings for Trump, strong evangelical turnout could help the party limit losses driven by voter frustration over the cost of living and the war in Iran.

That loyalty was on display last week at Village Church, an evangelical congregation in Blythewood, South Carolina, where hundreds of worshippers gathered for a weekly “Bible and Politics” sermon by Pastor Erik Estep. The backdrop: an unexpectedly competitive race for a Republican-held US Senate seat.

Speaking in the main worship hall, framed by a giant video screen and concert-style lighting, Estep did not endorse a candidate or party. But as he spoke against gambling, following sermons on abortion and socialism, he urged his predominantly white parishioners to view politics through a biblical lens.

"I believe the church is the bulwark of truth for our nation," Estep said from the stage. "And it will take people like you and churches like this church to protect this nation spiritually and morally."

The message resonated with Karen Whiting, a 72-year-old retired pharmaceutical executive who plans to vote for Republican Darline Graham over Annie Andrews, the Democrat. Graham was appointed by the governor to fill the seat of her late brother, Senator Lindsey Graham.

Whiting cited concerns that Democrats would allow transgender girls and women to compete in female sports, echoing other white evangelicals Reuters interviewed in South Carolina last week who prioritized social and religious issues over economic concerns.

Andrews, however, said in a recent campaign ad that she opposes transgender women competing in women's sports and gender-affirming surgeries for minors.

"I’m voting for biblical principles, and I do not believe the Democratic Party stands for biblical principles,” Whiting said. “Without God, this country’s going to fail.”

If visitors to Village Church needed more explicit guidance on how to vote, a candidate guide available in the church lobby left little doubt. Produced by the conservative Christian advocacy group Palmetto Family Council and distributed to churches across South Carolina, it awarded Graham green check marks on all seven issues it rated, including restrictions on abortion medication and gender-affirming care, while Andrews received mostly red X's.

In a sign of the Senate race's growing competitiveness, Trump campaigned for Graham at a Wednesday night rally at Clemson University in South Carolina, focusing much of his criticism on transgender issues and falsely accusing Andrews of supporting the "sexual mutilation" of children.

Andrews offered a different reading of evangelical voters’ priorities. In a statement to Reuters, she said she had visited evangelical churches and met voters of various faiths, political persuasions and backgrounds, finding that they were chiefly concerned about the economy. “They're struggling with the cost of everything. That's why I'm running,” she said.

STRONG BONDS

Reuters/Ipsos polling shows Trump's support among white evangelicals fell to 63% this month from 77% in January 2025. The decline is slightly smaller than his drop among the electorate as a whole, from 47% to 31%, and white evangelicals remain the only major demographic group tracked by Reuters/Ipsos where his support tops 60%.

The thrice-married Trump's bond with white evangelicals has survived a decade of scandals and investigations, including dozens of allegations of sexual misconduct, which he denies, and a hush-money case involving a porn star. The question for Republicans is whether economic pressures and unhappiness over the Iran war, now in its eighth month, are weakening that bond.

Reuters interviews with 15 people at two South Carolina churches suggested that his hold on white evangelical voters remained strong. At Village Church and Carolina Baptist Church in the city of Spartanburg, about a 90-minute drive from Blythewood, only 2 of the 15 said they were considering Andrews, and none indicated they were abandoning Trump.

While several voiced frustration with the Iran conflict and rising gas prices, most said they trusted Trump to keep Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon or, like Trump, blamed inflation on policies enacted under Democratic President Joe Biden.

Chad Connelly, an evangelical activist who heads the Christian voter-engagement group Faith Wins, said that while evangelicals "don't like paying higher prices," they are equally animated by social issues. Concerns about transgender athletes are "really playing everywhere" across the nearly two dozen states he has visited this election cycle, he said.

White evangelicals' loyalty to Trump reflects what Robert P. Jones, president of the Public Religion Research Institute, a nonprofit organization that studies religion and politics, calls a "grand bargain" forged during the 2016 election.

Many evangelicals have overlooked his personal conduct in exchange for his commitment to curtail abortion and LGBTQ rights, advance a conservative Christian vision of American life and pursue strict immigration policies that some supporters see as preserving the country's white Christian identity, Jones said.

"That has proven to be more powerful for this group than what they're having to pay at the gas pump," Jones, who has written extensively about the rise of Christian nationalism in American politics, told Reuters.

WHY EVANGELICALS MATTER

White evangelicals make up about 13% of US adults but nearly a third of Trump's winning coalition in 2024, according to a PRRI survey and a validated-voter analysis by the nonpartisan Pew Research Center. More than 80% voted for Trump in each of his three presidential campaigns, according to Pew. They differ sharply from Black Protestant evangelicals, who overwhelmingly support Democrats.

Evangelicals' loyalty could also prove pivotal in Senate races beyond South Carolina that may help determine control of Congress, including in Iowa and Kansas, where white evangelicals make up a significant share of the electorate.

Opinion polls suggest the race in South Carolina is close. This week Trafalgar Group, a Republican-leaning pollster, released a survey showing Andrews trailing Graham by 3 percentage points.

Part of Graham's challenge stems from lingering unease among some conservatives over her appointment to the Senate seat. Even after a boost from Trump, the political newcomer only narrowly defeated US Representative Ralph Norman in the party's August runoff, underscoring questions among some Republicans about her experience and conservative credentials.

A spokesperson for the Graham campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Yet even evangelicals lukewarm on Graham, like 53-year-old Kevin Thomas, said they felt they had little choice. Thomas, who attended the Village Church sermon and backed Norman, said he nevertheless did not trust Andrews on transgender issues.

“I’m leaning towards holding my nose and voting for Graham,” Thomas said. "I’m not willing to sacrifice six years of having a Democrat representing us in South Carolina."

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: US Justice Department threatens California over alleged noncitizen voters, letters show
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department on Tuesday gave California officials 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action, according to two letters reviewed by Reuters, part of an unprecedented effort to find evidence of voter fraud ahead of next month's elections.

The letters, written by acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter and addressed to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan, say the Justice Department provided officials in Los Angeles County with a "password-protected thumb drive" with the names of people the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens" and were sent mail-in ballots from California.

The letters demand that the state and county segregate returned mail-in ballots from voters on the Justice Department's list and not tabulate their votes "until citizenship has been determined." In cases where ballots have not been sent out yet, it orders California officials to withhold them from those on the list until their citizenship is confirmed.

The federal government "will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," according to the letters, if state and county officials do not follow its instructions.

"Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes," McCotter wrote.

The letters mark an escalation of the Trump administration's attempts to pressure states over alleged voting by non-US citizens and signal the Justice Department may be prepared to challenge ballots in the weeks leading up to the November 3 election, when Republicans will be defending their narrow majorities in Congress.

Justice Department spokeswoman Kiersten Pels confirmed the existence of the letters in a statement to Reuters, adding: "The department will take all necessary legal action to protect election integrity and ensure compliance with federal law.”

Representatives from the White House and the California secretary of state's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Logan also did not immediately respond.

FRAUD CLAIMS

The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that voting by non-US citizens is widespread, despite multiple studies showing it is rare.

Though states may have added more than 30,000 noncitizens to their voter rolls since 2000 due to software glitches and clerical errors, Reuters found in September, it was unclear how many had cast a ballot. Experts said the numbers were too small relative to the country’s 170 million registered voters to affect elections.

In July, the Justice Department sent letters to chief election officials in all 50 states warning they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls or cast ballots.

The department's Civil Rights Division has demanded nonpublic voter data, including voters' Social Security numbers or dates of birth, from nearly all states as part of its hunt for noncitizens on state rolls. It has sued 30 Democratic- and Republican-led states that refused to hand over their rolls, but has lost 26 of those cases without winning one.

Reuters reported last month that the Department of Homeland Security was using a commercial data broker to find sensitive voter information not included in publicly available rolls, which officials and experts warned could lead to citizens being falsely flagged as illegal voters and potentially detained.

Federal prosecutors have also ramped up prosecutions of noncitizens for allegedly voting in past elections or submitting fraudulent registrations, touting 16 new criminal cases on Monday.

Officials in Democratic-led California have tussled for months with the Trump administration over its attempts to intervene in election procedures over allegations of voter fraud.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin informed California officials on July 16 that the federal government believed the state had noncitizens on its voting rolls, according to the letter.

California could prove pivotal in deciding control of the US House of Representatives, especially after the state's voters approved a new congressional map that heavily favors Democrats as part of a nationwide redistricting sprint that began in Republican-led states.

Voters in Los Angeles will also weigh in on a ballot measure that would allow certain noncitizen legal residents to cast ballots in municipal elections.

items.title: Lawmakers say US briefing showed Russia targeting Democrats with misinformation
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 21 (Reuters) - The top Democratic lawmakers on the congressional intelligence committees on Wednesday said they received an intelligence briefing that Russia has been waging a misinformation campaign against Democrats running in next month's midterm elections.

The comments by Senator Mark Warner and Representative Jim Himes come as Republican President Donald Trump has in recent weeks eased economic sanctions on Russia and increased pressure on Ukraine to end its fight against Russian forces.

Warner and Himes told reporters they were limited in revealing what they had learned in an election security briefing that they had requested from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton because it was classified.

But, they said, Russia was waging the same kind of online misinformation campaign that the US intelligence community had tracked in US elections in 2016, 2020, and 2024.

"And the state of play, I would argue, is that, you know, Russia, similar to prior occasions, is going after Democrats," Warner said.

He noted news reports that Democrat James Talarico, who is running for the US Senate in Texas, and Senator Jon Ossoff, who is seeking re-election in Georgia, "in particular are being dinged" by fake advertisements created with AI.

The White House and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Russian embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Moscow in the past has denied meddling in US elections.

Himes said the pair could not provide details of the misinformation spread by Russia because the material was classified. But he added that Moscow's conduct has been "the same old, same old."

"The Russians are kind of throwing everything out there," said Himes. "Chaos, you know, don't trust your voting machines."

He added there was "no reason to believe" that China has not been conducting "extremely targeted" efforts as it has done in the past to influence voters.

Beijing has previously denied interfering in US elections and the Chinese Embassy in Washington on Wednesday described Himes' comment as "a false allegation and serious smear that has long been proved to be unfounded."

Recent Reuters/Ipsos polling has shown Democrats leading Republicans on the generic congressional ballot by high single digits to low double digits nationally, bolstering Democratic hopes of regaining control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate.

The lawmakers said they were concerned that Trump could pursue efforts to contest election results, including by claiming foreign hacking of voting infrastructure.

Himes emphasized that there was no evidence that any country could penetrate US election systems and change results.

"Nothing out there suggests that there is even the capability or the intent to do interference, whereas there is a pretty robust influence environment," said Himes.

items.title: Republicans fly past former spending caps nixed by US Supreme Court
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Since the US Supreme Court in June struck down federal caps on political party spending with input from candidates, Republican committees have surged past the former limits by more than $126 million while their Democratic counterparts have topped them by more than $46 million ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans are seeking to retain control of Congress in the midterms. Coordinated spending by Republican and Democratic committees from July through September was nearly eight times what they spent during the same months of the last midterm elections in 2022.

Republican and Democratic committees supporting candidates in races for the House of Representatives and Senate disclosed their coordinated spending totals for September in filings on Tuesday night to the Federal Election Commission.

In July, August and September — the three months since the court's ruling — the Republican committees poured a total of about $137 million of coordinated spending into House and Senate races across the country, according to their filings. Their Democratic counterparts spent a total of around $55 million during this period in coordinated spending, the filings showed.

Justice Elena Kagan, one of the nine-member court's three liberals, in remarks on Tuesday criticized its conservative majority for failing to appreciate the real-world impact of striking down coordinated spending limits.

"The people of America look around this political system and think that all this money, chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they're right," Kagan told an audience at Catholic University's law school in Washington.

The Supreme Court, in a 6-3 ruling on June 30 powered by its conservative majority, rejected coordinated-spending restrictions, agreeing with challengers including Trump's Vice President JD Vance that the limits violated the US Constitution's First Amendment protections against government abridgment of freedom of speech.

Republican committees have sought to use newly unlimited coordinated spending to help level the playing field in key races in which individual Democratic candidates had outraised their Republican opponents, according to political analysts.

A NEW FCC POLICY

More than two in three dollars of recent coordinated spending, or $129 million, by Republicans and Democrats came in September, when party committees gained access to discounted TV and radio advertising rates long available to political candidates under a new Federal Communications Commission policy.

The FCC, which currently has a 2-1 Republican majority, extended its so-called "lowest unit charge" rule in March to include party committees, a move seen as a boost to Republicans.

The Supreme Court twice intervened in recent weeks to stymie challenges to the FCC policy brought by Democratic candidates, handing a legal victory to Republican committees, whose coordinated spending in September was around two-thirds higher than that of their Democratic counterparts.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee, or NRSC, was one of the challengers in the case decided in June by the Supreme Court. It supports Republican Senate candidates, while the National Republican Congressional Committee, or NRCC, supports the party's House candidates. Both can accept funding from the Republican National Committee.

These three national Republican committees ended September with about $187 million in cash and $20 million in debt, according to FEC filings. Their Democratic counterparts held roughly $100 million and carried nearly $15 million in debt.

A 1971 US law called the Federal Election Campaign Act imposed contribution limits and other restrictions on campaign spending, with the aim of preventing corruption. Under it, spending by a political party to advocate for or against a candidate that was not coordinated with a candidate's campaign was considered an "independent expenditure" — and was not subject to a cap.

Spending coordinated between a party and a campaign was restricted. Before the Supreme Court's ruling, the 2026 limits had ranged from $130,600 to about $4.1 million for Senate candidates and from $65,300 to $130,600 for House candidates, depending on a state's population.

items.title: Republicans bet Musk’s millions can rescue Texas' Paxton in US Senate race
items.content_html:
HOUSTON, Texas, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Texas Democrats' best chance at a statewide win in more than three decades is facing a wall of Republican money, with Elon Musk and other donors pouring hundreds of millions into a late effort to rescue Senate candidate Ken Paxton.

With two weeks until the November 3 election and early voting under way, however, it is unclear how much impact the spending can still have. Polls show few undecided voters remain, and Republicans say their biggest challenge is turning out their own voters, many of whom are frustrated by the cost of living and the war with Iran launched by President Donald Trump, who has endorsed Paxton.

"The money being spent now isn't for persuasion. It's for mobilization," said pollster James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas. "In most of the statewide polling we've seen, Republicans are suffering from an enthusiasm gap."

Republican strategists say internal polling shows that gap has narrowed considerably.

"We've seen it collapse, thank God. It was one of our concerns," said Dave Carney, a longtime Republican strategist and chief adviser to Texas Governor Greg Abbott.

That turnout challenge helps explain the tone of Republican advertising. Rather than focusing on inflation and the economy, which polls consistently show are among voters' top concerns, Republicans in Texas and other battleground states have leaned heavily on culture-war themes to energize their base.

Republican groups have spent more than $100 million nationally since August 1 on more than 200 ads accusing Democrats of backing “sex change” procedures for children, according to an analysis of AdImpact data by FactCheck.org.

TEXAS-SIZED SPENDING

Combined advertising spending in the race between Paxton, the state's Republican attorney general, and Democrat James Talarico has topped $500 million, according to ad-tracking data, putting it on pace to become the most expensive US Senate contest ever.

Talarico has held a small but consistent lead over Paxton, though generally within the margin of error, making it Texas' most competitive statewide race since 1994, Henson said.

Outside groups backing Paxton have spent about $239 million, more than five times the roughly $45 million spent by the largest Democratic-aligned groups. Texas PAC, a Republican super PAC, alone has accounted for nearly $149 million.

The group was launched by the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican Senate super PAC.

Musk, who lives in Texas and has relocated SpaceX, Tesla, X and other businesses there, has contributed $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, which subsequently transferred matching sums to Texas PAC, according to federal filings.

Talarico has offset the outside-spending disadvantage with grassroots fundraising. His campaign says it raised $64 million from July through September, more than triple Paxton's total, with 97% of donations under $100.

He spent $61 million on ads through September, according to AdImpact, while the biggest Democratic outside group, Lone Star Rising PAC, has spent $19.3 million.

The influx of Republican money arrived relatively late in the campaign, with Trump's MAGA Inc. super PAC not beginning major spending until early September.

"I think the cavalry arrived just in the nick of time for Paxton," said Republican donor and oil businessman Dan Eberhart.

GOING NEGATIVE

Much of that spending has funded attacks portraying Talarico as out of step with Texas voters on culture-war issues. Independent fact checkers say the ads distort Talarico's record, and Henson said their goal is “arousing negative sentiment among Republican voters” to boost turnout.

Texas PAC ads tell voters that Talarico is "for they/them, not you" and accuse him of supporting taxpayer-funded sex-change surgeries for minors. PolitiFact rated that claim false, noting that while Talarico opposed a 2023 ban on gender-transition care for minors, he has said he opposes gender-reassignment surgery for children.

A Paxton campaign ad featured an AI-generated Talarico reading from a fictional "King James (Talarico) Bible" that combined excerpts of his past remarks, including one describing God as "nonbinary." FactCheck.org said the ad lacked key context.

Talarico has responded by casting Paxton as "the most corrupt politician in Texas."

Paxton was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House in 2023 on abuse-of-office allegations but was acquitted by the state Senate. Separate state securities-fraud charges dating to 2015 were dropped in 2024 under an agreement requiring community service, ethics training and restitution. Paxton denied wrongdoing.

The Paxton campaign did not respond to requests for comment. It has previously said Talarico raises the allegations to distract from his own record.

Some voters say the Republican attacks are unconvincing.

Sal Anthony Rodriguez, a 32-year-old Houston operations manager who voted for Trump in 2020 and 2024, said he now supports Talarico, partly because of what he views as misleading attacks.

"I've seen a lot of ads saying that he is in 100% support for transgender surgeries on kids, and a quick Google search showed that that was not accurate," Rodriguez said.

Democrats argue the focus on cultural issues reflects Republican difficulty addressing voters' economic concerns.

"Voters are really pissed off about the state of their lives right now, and you can only run so many trans ads at people who are sick of paying $6 for diesel," said Chuck Rocha, a senior adviser to the Talarico campaign.

items.title: How the Republican redistricting gambit faltered under Trump slump
items.content_html:
Oct 21 (Reuters) - At President Donald Trump's urging, Republicans pursued an unprecedented mid-decade redistricting campaign ahead of November's midterm elections, redrawing dozens of US House of Representatives districts in an effort to preserve their narrow majority.

With less than two weeks until Election Day, however, Trump's unpopularity has wiped out most of those gains, leaving Republicans scrambling to defend even districts they engineered to be safely conservative.

As of June, Republicans had increased their advantage in 16 redrawn districts. Today, nine of those Republican-leaning districts are either expected to go to Democrats or are too close to call, according to a Reuters analysis of ratings from leading election forecasters. A 10th Republican district was thrown out by courts.

Redistricting typically occurs only once a decade following the US Census' population count. But Texas Republicans tore up the state's existing US House map last summer with Trump's backing, setting off a multistate fight between the parties that Republicans appeared to win handily. Democrats were only able to use redistricting to gain an edge in six districts.

But what looked like a Republican victory has since been undercut by Trump's record-low approval rating, driven by the unpopular war in Iran and Americans' deep frustration with the resulting high gas prices.

"It's a powerful lesson that you can be too smart for your own good when you try to predict the future," said Michael Li, a redistricting expert at New York University's Brennan Center for Justice.

TEXAS, FLORIDA RACES NO LONGER SAFE BETS

Most of the Republican gains were expected to come from Texas and Florida, where new maps reshaped nine Democratic-held seats into districts that Trump carried in 2024 by anywhere from 9 to 20 percentage points.

But the collapse of Trump's support among Latino voters has upended the political calculus in those states. Analysts now view only one of those nine as a sure thing for Republicans, with six considered highly competitive.

"I think the maps in Texas and Florida were way too confident that Hispanic voters would continue to vote for Republicans at the same level they did in 2024," said Erin Covey, who analyzes US House races for the Cook Political Report. "There is absolutely a world where Republicans don't flip any of the four seats they redrew in Florida."

The median outcome for Republicans is a gain of around three seats from redistricting alone, Covey said. But if the Democratic wave turns into a tsunami, she added, Democrats could actually end up netting two seats through redistricting.

That said, the national House map is objectively better for Republicans than it was prior to redistricting, according to Jacob Rubashkin, an analyst at Inside Elections.

"The number of pickups is almost certain to fall well below expectation," he said. "It's also true that Republicans will still do better because they redistricted than had they lived and let live."

Some of the newly redrawn districts are among the races that have drawn the most campaign spending, underscoring their competitiveness. Four of the six House races that have received the most outside spending from Republican-aligned groups - an average of more than $12 million each - are taking place in Republican-redistricted seats, according to campaign finance data.

Democrats need to flip at least four House seats on November 3 to win control of the chamber.

DEMOCRATS REACH DEEP INTO REPUBLICAN TERRITORY

Even districts that once seemed unassailable are potentially in reach for Democrats.

After the US Supreme Court in April hollowed out the Voting Rights Act's protections for districts with large minority populations, Alabama Republicans quickly dismantled one of the state's two predominantly Black districts in favor of a new, majority-white one that backed Trump by more than 14 percentage points in 2024.

But now, two national forecasters, Inside Elections and Sabato's Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia, both categorize the race as "Lean Republican," suggesting incumbent Democrat Shomari Figures could prevail in a strong Democratic wave.

To be sure, Democrats may not carry every seat they redrew either. In California, where Democratic lawmakers passed a new map targeting five Republican-held seats, two Republicans are locked in tight contests with Democratic challengers, according to analysts.

In some cases, the new maps could also have unintended consequences for incumbent Republicans.

Under the updated Texas map, the seat of Republican Monica De La Cruz remained solidly Republican, with Trump winning the district's voters by nearly 18 percentage points. But most of that territory was new to her, forcing the incumbent to introduce herself to swaths of new voters.

Her Democratic opponent, Bobby Pulido, is a well-known Tejano music star who has sought to transform his cultural popularity into political success. That seat is now widely seen as a tossup.

items.title: Three issues defining the 2026 US midterm elections
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, October 20 - President Donald Trump’s record-low popularity, voter frustration over the cost of living and a fierce immigration fight are shaping the November 3 midterm elections, which will determine whether Republicans keep control of Congress or Democrats gain the power to challenge his administration.

Republicans hold narrow majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of each chamber.

The outcome will hinge on a relatively small number of competitive races, but the campaigns are being shaped nationally by Trump himself and voter concerns over affordability and immigration.

Here is a look at the three issues defining the election:

DONALD TRUMP

The president has put himself front and center in the closing stretch of the campaign cycle despite his record-low popularity, with upcoming rallies in Florida, Iowa, Michigan and Texas. Trump's approval rating has fallen to an all-time low 31%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll. Yet he has repeatedly urged voters to pretend he's on the ballot, an effort that could motivate Democrats and independents to rally against his party despite the message being aimed at increasing turnout among Trump's base.

Democrats have said Trump has broken his campaign promises to lower costs and end wars. They have vowed to tackle an affordability agenda to reduce Americans' cost of living and hold the administration accountable for alleged corruption if voters give them control of either chamber.

AFFORDABILITY

Voters have consistently ranked the cost of living as the top issue this election cycle. Half of registered voters surveyed in a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll cited the cost of living as the most important factor in how they will vote. In the same poll, voters highlighted healthcare, gasoline, food and housing as the top household bills lawmakers should focus on.

Republicans' top legislative achievement was a tax cut extension that slashed roughly $1 trillion in spending for Medicaid, the government health insurance program for low-income Americans, and other health programs. Democrats last year forced a government shutdown over a failed effort to extend expiring health subsidies that benefited 24 million Americans.

Gas prices have spiked since the US and Israel launched military strikes on Iran in February. The national average price of gas is $4.28 — $1.20 higher than it was a year ago, according to AAA. The average cost of diesel is $6.32 — a $2.70 increase from a year earlier.

Grocery costs are up 1.8% over the past year, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics data on consumer prices. Federal Housing Finance Agency data show home prices rose 2.1% over the past year. Congress passed a bipartisan housing bill earlier this year. It became law without Trump's signature.

IMMIGRATION

Preliminary data from the Department of Homeland Security showed a 95% drop in migrants apprehended at the southwest border compared to former President Joe Biden's administration. The agency said there have been no Border Patrol releases the entire fiscal year for the first time ever.

But fatal encounters with federal immigration agents have occurred in Maine, Minnesota and Texas. The backlash to the death of two US citizens in Minnesota pulled many Democrats in competitive primaries to the left this year, with some candidates calling for the impeachment of then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and others saying Immigration and Customs Enforcement should be abolished.

Democrats and Republicans sparred over immigration funding this year in a stalemate that forced Republicans to unilaterally pass a $70 billion bill to fund ICE and the Border Patrol for the remainder of Trump's presidency. Republicans counter Democrats' criticism by saying Democrats support open borders.

Federal immigration officials also raided the Washington home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota this month, drawing widespread condemnation from Democrats. A person familiar with the case against Omar told Reuters one potential aim of the investigation could be to strip her of US citizenship and deport her.

OTHER ISSUES

Artificial intelligence and data centers, cryptocurrency, abortion and Israel could also influence voters in individual races. In Ohio's Senate race, for example, Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown has labeled Republican Senator Jon Husted the face of data centers, and the crypto super PAC Defend American Jobs has spent more than $46 million to reelect Husted over Brown, a former US senator who chaired the chamber's Banking Committee.

In Maine's Senate race, Democratic nominee Troy Jackson is hoping voters don't forget that Republican Senator Susan Collins helped confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, which later overturned the federal right to abortion. Collins is on the election ballot for the first time since the high court made abortion a state issue rather than a federal right.

In Michigan, Republican nominee Mike Rogers has indicated he would accept help from a pro-Israel super PAC that spent more than $30 million backing Democratic US Representative Haley Stevens in her unsuccessful primary against Abdul El-Sayed, who now faces Rogers in the general election. The group has already spent more than $280,000 on mailers against El-Sayed.

Earlier this week, Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection.

items.title: US judge dismisses Sam Altman's sister's sexual abuse lawsuit
items.content_html:
Oct 20 (Reuters) - Sam Altman on Tuesday won the dismissal of a civil lawsuit filed by his sister accusing the OpenAI co-founder and chief executive of repeated sexual abuse more than two decades ago, an accusation he denies.

In dismissing Annie Altman's lawsuit, US District Judge Zachary Bluestone wrote that she had refused to appear for an independent medical examination despite warnings that failure to do so would result in the case's dismissal.

Laura Politi, a lawyer for Annie Altman, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Santos Perez, a lawyer who previously represented Annie Altman in the case but withdrew this month, said in a statement, "I am no longer authorized to comment on this case but I continue to believe in Annie."

Lawyers for Sam Altman did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Sam Altman became a face of the artificial intelligence boom after the chatbot ChatGPT was released in 2022.

Annie Altman brought her lawsuit in St. Louis, Missouri, federal court in January 2025.

She accused her brother of sexually abusing and raping her between 1997 and 2006 at the family home in suburban Clayton, Missouri, starting when she was 3 and he was 12. She said the last acts of sexual abuse and rape occurred when Sam Altman was an adult. He is now 41.

The Altman family has said Annie Altman has mental health challenges and received financial support. Sam Altman has said she began accusing him on social media of sexual abuse after the family rejected her demands for more funds.
